meta.purpose: Controlled vocabulary for jewelry design app parameter dropdowns and AI prompt compiler.
meta.source: GIA colored gemstone color/clarity standards, extracted and paraphrased from user-provided reference document plus web research for stone families not in that source.
meta.note: Diamond D-to-Z scale is already a standard linear system and does not require extraction here.

type_ii.label: Usually included
type_ii.market_expectation: Minor eye-visible inclusions are common and accepted

type_iii.label: Almost always included
type_iii.market_expectation: Visible inclusions ("jardin") accepted; color outweighs clarity

non_applicable.label: Organic or amorphous gems — graded by an entirely different model, see the pearl and opal sections
non_applicable.market_expectation: Valued on luster, surface, or play-of-color, not internal clarity

gia_diamond.meaning: Flawless, no inclusions or blemishes visible at 10x
Internally flawless, only surface blemishes at 10x
Very very slightly included, extremely difficult to see at 10x
Very very slightly included, very difficult to see at 10x
Very slightly included, difficult to see at 10x
Very slightly included, somewhat easy to see at 10x
Slightly included, easy to see at 10x
Slightly included, very easy to see at 10x, may be eye-visible
Included, obvious, affects transparency and durability

ruby.meaning: top-grade ruby red, glows under UV
ruby.origin_tie: named for the Mogok, Burma benchmark

ruby.meaning: deeper red, no glow, still top-tier

sapphire_blue.gia: vivid deep blue, slight violet, tone 6-7
sapphire_blue.meaning: deepest, most saturated blue sapphire grade
sapphire_blue.origin_tie: named for the Mogok, Burma benchmark

sapphire_blue.meaning: soft, bright blue, named after the flower
sapphire_blue.origin_tie: associated with Sri Lanka, Madagascar stones

sapphire_blue.meaning: vivid reflective blue between Cornflower and Royal
silk inclusions scatter light for a velvety look
sapphire_blue.origin_tie: the hallmark of legendary Kashmir sapphires

sapphire_blue.gia: dark tone, lower saturation, gray cast
sapphire_blue.meaning: denim-blue, lower trade value than metamorphic blues
sapphire_blue.origin_tie: basalt-hosted stones from Australia, Thailand, Nigeria

sapphire_fancy.gia: pinkish orange to orangey pink, pastel, low-med saturation
sapphire_fancy.meaning: rarest fancy sapphire color, named after the lotus flower
sapphire_fancy.notes: watch for tenebrescence — some pink sapphires fake this color temporarily under UV

emerald.gia: highly saturated deep green, yellowish nuance
emerald.meaning: vivid color even in small sizes
emerald.origin_tie: named for the Sandawana mines, Zimbabwe

aquamarine.gia: intensely saturated deep blue, no green/gray cast
aquamarine.origin_tie: named for the Santa Maria mine, Brazil — now used by color match anywhere

aquamarine.gia: same deep blue profile as Santa Maria
aquamarine.meaning: African stones matching the Brazilian benchmark
aquamarine.origin_tie: named for African (Mozambique) source, referencing the original Brazil color

spinel.gia: highly saturated neon pink to hot, slightly orangey red
spinel.meaning: glows under both UV and daylight, always untreated
spinel.origin_tie: sourced from Man Sin and Namya, Burma

spinel.gia: vivid blue to electric royal blue
spinel.meaning: colored by cobalt, stays bright rather than dark/grayish
spinel.origin_tie: Luc Yen, Vietnam and Mahenge, Tanzania
spinel.notes: cobalt-diffused treated fakes exist at steep discount

tourmaline.gia: vivid violetish blue to bluish green, neon, medium-high saturation
tourmaline.meaning: the most valuable tourmaline color, glows with a neon quality
tourmaline.origin_tie: named for Paraiba, Brazil — copper-bearing material from Mozambique and Nigeria now trades under the same name
tourmaline.notes: colored by copper + manganese; this is what separates it from iron-colored blue/green tourmaline

tourmaline.gia: blue-green to green-blue, medium to vivid saturation
tourmaline.meaning: tropical lagoon color, a lower-cost look-alike to Paraiba
tourmaline.notes: colored by iron, not copper — the key distinction from true Paraiba despite the similar color; finest material from Namibia

tourmaline.origin_tie: named for its canary-bird color; also the name of a key mining concession in Zambia
tourmaline.notes: usually heat-treated from brownish rough to reach vivid yellow

tourmaline.gia: pink to red, purplish red, must hold color under multiple light sources
tourmaline.meaning: the red/hot-pink grade — must stay red in daylight, LED, and incandescent light, or it's just "pink tourmaline"
tourmaline.notes: sourced from Brazil, Nigeria, Mozambique, Madagascar

tourmaline.gia: dark violetish blue, blue, or greenish blue

tourmaline.meaning: the deepest tourmaline green, priced as a tsavorite alternative
tourmaline.notes: colored by vanadium and/or chromium; shows red under a Chelsea filter, unlike ordinary iron-colored green tourmaline

tourmaline.gia: pink core, green rind — bi-color zoning
tourmaline.meaning: the classic bi-color tourmaline, cut in slices to show the pattern
tourmaline.notes: natural color zoning, not a treatment; usually cut as polished slices rather than faceted

garnet.gia: vivid green, medium tone, high saturation
garnet.meaning: the finest, most brilliant green garnet — an emerald alternative with more fire
garnet.origin_tie: named for Tsavo National Park, Kenya, where it was first mined commercially
garnet.notes: colored by vanadium/chromium; never treated; rare over 2ct

garnet.gia: olive to emerald green, very high dispersion
garnet.meaning: the antique garnet grade — more fire than a diamond
garnet.notes: wispy "horsetail" inclusions are a prized authenticity marker, not a flaw, especially in Russian material; colored by chromium

garnet.gia: purplish red to violet-red, medium-light tone
garnet.meaning: the soft rose-violet red garnet grade
garnet.notes: pyrope-almandine mix; typically eye-clean, unlike most Type II garnets

garnet.meaning: the finest vivid orange spessartite grade
garnet.origin_tie: trade name born from a famous 1990s Kunene River, Namibia find
garnet.notes: brighter, purer orange than hessonite; less pink than malaya

garnet.meaning: warm peach-orange, between rhodolite and spessartite in color
garnet.origin_tie: closely tied to the Umba Valley, Tanzania, its original source
garnet.notes: name means "outcast" in Swahili — miners rejected it at first for not fitting known categories

garnet.meaning: warm cinnamon-orange, softer than mandarin garnet
garnet.notes: classic swirly "heat-wave" internal texture; long history in Vedic astrology as "Gomed"

garnet.meaning: pastel mint-green grossular, a lighter cousin to tsavorite
garnet.origin_tie: named for the Merelani Hills, Tanzania — the same source as tanzanite

garnet.gia: blue-green in daylight, shifts to purplish red in incandescent light

chrysoberyl.gia: green to bluish-green in daylight, red to purplish-red in incandescent light
chrysoberyl.meaning: the definitive color-change stone — "emerald by day, ruby by night"
chrysoberyl.notes: graded by percentage of color shift (5-100%); Russia (Ural Mtns) and Brazil (Hematita mine) are the premium origins; rare cat's-eye alexandrite shows both phenomena at once

chrysoberyl.meaning: when the trade says "cat's-eye" with no other name attached, it always means chrysoberyl — the finest chatoyant gem
chrysoberyl.origin_tie: Sri Lanka is the benchmark source
chrysoberyl.notes: graded on eye sharpness, centering, and the "milk-and-honey" effect — one half of the dome reads milky, the other honey-gold

tanzanite.gia: violetish blue to bluish violet, best graded vB 6/6
tanzanite.origin_tie: named for Tanzania — its only commercial source worldwide, an 8-square-mile deposit
tanzanite.notes: over 95% of material is heat-treated to remove a brownish veil, which is standard and accepted; AAA-AAAA grading is informal trade shorthand with no lab standard behind it — treat retailer grade claims with caution

topaz.meaning: the rarest, most valuable topaz color, prized for a reddish pleochroic flash
topaz.origin_tie: Ouro Preto, Brazil is the primary and historic source
topaz.notes: pink/red comes from chromium and is natural; yellow/orange base tones are sometimes heat-enhanced

topaz.meaning: named for the color of sherry wine, a step below Imperial in rarity
the darkest of the three blue topaz trade grades
topaz.origin_tie: named for the city, not a source location
topaz.notes: virtually 100% irradiation-treated; this is industry-standard and disclosed, not a red flag

topaz.gia: medium, bright, electric blue, no grey
topaz.meaning: the mid-tone blue topaz grade, most common in commercial jewelry
the lightest blue topaz grade — the only shade with a natural, untreated counterpart, though most on the market is still treated for consistent supply

topaz.gia: not a color grade — a rainbow iridescent coating
topaz.meaning: colorless topaz coated with a thin metallic film
topaz.notes: a surface treatment, not a natural color; flag separately from hue/tone/saturation parameters since the coating can wear

zircon.gia: vivid blue, sometimes with a greenish secondary hue
zircon.meaning: the most popular zircon color, valued for diamond-like fire and dispersion
zircon.origin_tie: virtually all commercial material comes from Ratanakiri Province, Cambodia
zircon.notes: rough is brown; heat treatment at 900-1000°C produces the blue; untreated blue zircon essentially does not exist in the trade and needs no special disclosure

beryl_other.gia: light pink to rose to peach
beryl_other.meaning: pink beryl, named for financier J.P. Morgan
beryl_other.notes: manganese-colored; often heat-treated to remove yellow patches

beryl_other.meaning: golden beryl, Greek for "gift of the sun"
the clear beryl — mainly a collector's stone, rarely used in fine jewelry since white sapphire and diamond outperform it optically
beryl_other.origin_tie: named for Goshen, Massachusetts, its original find site

beryl_other.meaning: the rarest gem-quality beryl — rarer than diamond
beryl_other.origin_tie: the only commercial source on Earth is the Wah Wah Mountains, Utah
beryl_other.notes: "Bixbite" is discouraged by trade bodies since it's easily confused with the unrelated mineral bixbyite — prefer "Red Beryl" in customer-facing copy

pearl.note: Pearls are organic, not crystalline — they carry no hue/tone/saturation code and no GIA Type I/II/III clarity. This needs its own parameter set, not the gemstone schema above.

trade_grading_scales.used_for: Akoya, freshwater, and often applied loosely to any pearl type
trade_grading_scales.notes: AAA is the top common commercial grade; special grades Hanadama and Tennyo sit above AAA for the finest akoya strands

trade_grading_scales.used_for: Tahitian and South Sea pearls specifically
trade_grading_scales.notes: A is finest (few surface marks, sharp luster), D is lowest; often cross-converted to AAA-A for retail customers

types.meaning: the classic white pearl — round, mirror-like luster
large, soft satin luster, white to silver
natural champagne to deep 24k-gold color, never dyed
the "black pearl" — actually shows peacock, green, blue, and aubergine overtones, never dyed
widest range of shapes and natural colors, most affordable
small, non-nucleated, all-nacre pearls formed as a byproduct of culturing — irregular baroque shapes, exceptionally high luster since there's no bead core

opal.note: Opals are amorphous silica, not crystalline — graded by body tone and play-of-color, not hue/tone/saturation. Needs its own parameter set.
opal.body_tone_scale: N1 (jet black) to N9 (white) — N1-N4 is called black opal, N5-N6 dark opal, N7-N9 white/light opal

types.meaning: the most valuable opal type — the dark background makes play-of-color pop
types.origin_tie: Lightning Ridge, Australia is the benchmark source, sometimes called "Lightning Ridge opal" in the trade
types.notes: red play-of-color on a black body tone is the rarest, most valuable combination

types.meaning: the most common opal type, softer pastel play-of-color
types.origin_tie: Coober Pedy, Australia is the largest source

types.gia: transparent to semi-transparent, any body tone
types.meaning: defined by clarity, not color — shows the most vivid, sharp play-of-color of any type
types.notes: can occur as black crystal or white crystal depending on body tone

types.meaning: thin veins of precious opal left attached to their natural ironstone host rock
types.notes: still classed as solid natural opal since the ironstone backing occurs naturally, not as an applied treatment

types.meaning: valued for vivid bodycolor, with or without play-of-color
types.origin_tie: also called "Mexican Opal" or "Mexican Fire Opal" in the trade

types.notes: hydrophane — absorbs water and can temporarily change appearance; trades at a discount to comparable Australian material for this instability

types.meaning: opal with no play-of-color at all
types.notes: usually the base material black or boulder opal forms within; not gem-grade on its own

phenomena.note: Optical effects that cut across many stone families. When present, these should layer on top of the stone's normal color parameters, not replace them.

chatoyancy_cats_eye.definition: a single band of light gliding across a cabochon, caused by parallel needle-like inclusions
chatoyancy_cats_eye.trade_convention: "Cat's-eye" with no qualifier always means chrysoberyl (cymophane) — the finest example. Every other stone must be named explicitly, e.g. "tourmaline cat's-eye."

stones.quality_marker: milk-and-honey effect, sharp centered eye — the gold standard
coarser, less sharp eye than chrysoberyl
most common and affordable cat's-eye material
extremely rare when combined with color-change — a double phenomenon, major value premium

asterism_star.definition: a 4, 6, or rarely 12-rayed star from intersecting sets of needle inclusions, always cut en cabochon
asterism_star.trade_convention: more rays generally means more value; a sharp, centered, mobile star outranks a faint or off-center one

stones.quality_marker: the most famous star stone; Sri Lanka and Myanmar are top sources
rarer and generally more valuable than star sapphire
only found in India and the Idaho Panhandle, USA
dark green to black body color
soft, subtle star, entry-level price point

color_change.definition: a shift in body color between daylight and incandescent light, from selective light absorption

stones.quality_marker: the definitive color-change stone; graded by percentage of shift, 5% to 100%
rare, mainly Madagascar — see garnet section above
a less dramatic shift than alexandrite

adularescence_labradorescence.definition: a floating sheen or flash of light from thin-layer light interference within the stone, distinct from chatoyancy and asterism

stones.quality_marker: a blue sheen on a colorless base is the finest grade, classically from Sri Lanka
broad flashes of blue, green, and gold; the finest material is called Spectrolite, from Finland

cuts_and_shapes.name: Marquise
cuts_and_shapes.meaning: pointed both ends, strong visual size

cuts_and_shapes.name: Princess
cuts_and_shapes.meaning: square, sharp corners, needs corner protection

cuts_and_shapes.name: Cushion
cuts_and_shapes.meaning: rounded square or rectangle with large facets, a softer vintage look, sometimes called "pillow cut"

cuts_and_shapes.name: Asscher
cuts_and_shapes.meaning: square step cut, deep geometric reflection

cuts_and_shapes.name: Cabochon
cuts_and_shapes.meaning: smooth dome, required for chatoyancy and asterism to display

cuts_and_shapes.name: Rose Cut
cuts_and_shapes.meaning: flat bottom, faceted dome, vintage glow

gaps_to_fill: Jadeite (Jade) — different grading system entirely (translucency, texture, Type A/B/C treatment), needs a dedicated source.
Crystal/Quartz trade names beyond what's covered (amethyst, citrine, ametrine) — low priority, decorative tier.
Diamond D-to-Z and Fancy Color grades — already standardized, hardcode directly.
Peridot, Iolite, Kunzite/Hiddenite — single-color stones, no major trade-term layer needed beyond GIA hue/tone/sat.

findings.note: Metalwork trade vocabulary for chains and clasps — extend here, never in code.

chain_styles.note: uniform round links, the everyday standard
twisted flattened links lying flat on the skin
curb pattern with alternating long links
smooth sleeve of plates, no visible links

clasp_types.note: bar through ring, decorative, easy one-handed
tongue into box, often with safety eight
easiest to use, add a safety chain for weight
open hook, antique look, light pieces only

species.note: Canonical species registry: sg (specific gravity) drives the carat-mm density check; clarity_systems, trade_color_keys, and allowed_phenomena point into the sections above. Jadeite deliberately absent — open item, needs a dedicated grading source.

shape_factors.note: Fraction of the stone's L×W×D bounding box its volume occupies; carat = L × W × D × SG × factor / 200. These are the standard gemological weight-estimation factors ×200 (round brilliant 0.0018 → 0.36).
